                      out.width = "100%")
find_proj_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(path)
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(path, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (parent == path) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", getwd())
    path <- parent
  }
}
proj_root <- find_proj_root()
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)
```

# Introduction

Building consents are permits issued by councils before building work can start. Stats NZ publishes, every month,
the number, declared value and floor area of the consents issued in each district, by building type. We use the
*Building consents issued: August 2026* release to answer three questions:

1. **RQ1 (regression):** What drives the real cost per m² of new houses across districts?
2. **RQ2 (clustering):** What kinds of building markets does New Zealand have?
3. **RQ3 (classification):** Will a district's consents rise or fall next year?

RQ1 is complete: data preparation, exploratory analysis, models and interpretation. The RQ2 and RQ3 sections are
still to be written.

# Data

## Source

* **Stats NZ, Building consents issued: August 2026** (CC BY 4.0): 13 CSV tables, 10.4 million rows in total.
  The main table for RQ1 is *Building consents by territorial authority (Monthly)*: 4.35 million rows, one row
  per series per month, covering 67 districts from April 1990 to August 2026.
* **Stats NZ, Business price indexes: June 2026 quarter**: the Capital Goods Price Index (CGPI) for
  dwelling units (series `CEPQ.S611011A`), used to convert dollars of the day into June-2026 dollars.
* A district-to-region lookup we compiled (67 districts → 16 regions).

## What one row means

Each row of the raw table is an *aggregate*, not an individual consent: for example, "Queenstown-Lakes District,
new houses, floor area, August 2026 = 13,139 m²". Building types are nested (houses ⊂ dwelling units ⊂ residential
buildings ⊂ all buildings), so values must never be summed across types. Floor area is recorded for new work only.

# Data preparation for RQ1

## Checks on the raw data

Before building anything we confirmed that the table is complete and internally consistent:

* the grid is complete (68 areas × 437 months, no missing values);
* every value has final status;
* dwelling units equal the sum of their four sub-types in every district-month;
* districts add up exactly to the New Zealand total for count, floor area and value; and
* our district-to-region lookup reproduces Stats NZ's regional totals to within 1.3% (nine regions exactly).

## From monthly records to a modelling table

```{r decisions}
tribble(
  ~Step, ~`What we did`, ~Why,
  "Unit of analysis", "District × quarter, complete quarters only (1990Q2–2026Q2)", "Monthly district counts are too small and noisy",
  "Scope", "New houses only; national total and 'area outside TA' removed", "Only houses have a consistent value and floor area per district",
  "GST", "Removed GST of the day (12.5% to Sep 2010, 15% after) and re-applied 15%", "Avoids a false +2.2% jump in 2010Q4",
  "Inflation", "Deflated by CGPI (dwelling units) to June-2026 dollars", "Compares every year on one price basis",
  "Small counts", "Rows with fewer than 5 new houses kept but not modelled", "A single unusual house dominates such a quarter",
  "Response", "log(real $ per m²) and relative cost vs the rest of NZ (see EDA)", "Multiplicative effects; isolates district differences",
  "Validation", "Train 1990–2019, test 2020–2026", "A random split would leak the national cycle"
) |> kable(caption = "Preparation decisions for RQ1")
```

## Removing inflation

```{r fig-cgpi, fig.cap = "Capital Goods Price Index for dwelling units vs all residential buildings, rescaled to June 2026 = 1."}
include_graphics(fig("fig01_cgpi"))
```

```{r fig-nz, fig.cap = "National consented value per m² of new houses, nominal vs real."}
include_graphics(fig("fig02_nz_nominal_vs_real"))
```

Nationally, the nominal value per m² of a new house rose from
$`r f0(nz$nominal[nz$year == 1991])` in 1991 to $`r f0(nz$nominal[nz$year == 2025])` in 2025
(×`r round(nz$nominal[nz$year == 2025] / nz$nominal[nz$year == 1991], 1)`). In June-2026 dollars the change is from
$`r f0(nz$real[nz$year == 1991])` to $`r f0(nz$real[nz$year == 2025])`,
or `r round(100 * (nz$real[nz$year == 2025] / nz$real[nz$year == 1991] - 1))`%. Almost all of the headline increase
is building-cost inflation; RQ1 is about what is left, especially the differences *between districts*.

## Small counts

```{r fig-funnel, fig.cap = "Real $/m² against the number of houses behind each district-quarter. The dashed line marks the 5-house minimum."}
include_graphics(fig("fig03_funnel_small_counts"))
```

`r sum(full$houses_n < 5)` of the `r f0(nrow(full))` district-quarters (`r round(100 * mean(full$houses_n < 5), 1)`%)
have fewer than five new houses. They are concentrated in a few small districts (Chatham Islands, Kawerau, Wairoa,
Waitomo) and give very unstable ratios, so they are excluded from modelling.

## The response variable

```{r fig-response, fig.cap = "Distribution of the response among modelled district-quarters."}
include_graphics(fig("fig04_response_distribution"))
```

Among the `r f0(nrow(model))` modelled district-quarters the median real cost is
$`r f0(median(model$real_cost_m2))` per m², with 98% of rows between
$`r f0(quantile(model$real_cost_m2, .01))` and $`r f0(quantile(model$real_cost_m2, .99))`.

## Candidate drivers

```{r features}
tribble(
  ~Feature, ~Meaning,
  "Average house size", "Floor area ÷ number of new houses (m²)",
  "Volume", "log(number of new houses in the quarter)",
  "Multi-unit share", "Share of new dwellings that are apartments, townhouses or retirement units",
  "Building intensity", "New dwellings in the past 12 months per 1,000 residents (from 1996)",
  "Growth", "Change in new houses vs the same quarter a year earlier",
  "Other activity", "Real value of residential alterations and of new non-residential building",
  "Location", "District, region, island, city vs district council",
  "Time", "Year, quarter, linear trend"
) |> kable(caption = "Candidate predictors of real $/m²")
```

No predictor is calculated from house *value*, which is the numerator of the response.

## Training and test sets

```{r split-table}
split |> rename(Set = split, Period = period, `All rows` = all_rows,
                `Modelled rows` = modelled_rows, Districts = districts_modelled) |>
  kable(caption = "Chronological train/test split")
```

```{r fig-split, fig.cap = "Modelled district-quarters per year in the training and test sets."}
include_graphics(fig("fig05_train_test_split"))

# RQ1: Exploratory analysis

All exploration uses the training years (1990–2019) only, so that nothing about the test years influences
modelling choices.

## Two ways to measure cost

Real $/m² mixes two things: the whole country getting dearer or cheaper over time, and some districts being
dearer than others. Because RQ1 is about districts, we also define a **relative cost**: the log of a district's
real $/m² minus the log of the real $/m² of *all other* districts in the same quarter. A value of +0.10 means
about 10% dearer than the rest of New Zealand at that time.

```{r var-expl}
ve <- tab("t05_variance_explained")
ve |> mutate(across(-grouping, ~ paste0(round(100 * .x), "%"))) |>
  rename(Grouping = grouping) |>
  kable(caption = "Share of variance explained by each grouping on its own (R², training rows)")
```

```{r fig-var, fig.cap = "Variance explained by place and time, for each response."}
include_graphics(fig("fig07_variance_explained"))
```

Time explains `r round(100 * ve[[2]][ve$grouping == "Quarter (time)"])`% of the variation in log real cost, and district
`r round(100 * ve[[2]][ve$grouping == "District"])`%. For relative cost, district explains
`r round(100 * ve[[3]][ve$grouping == "District"])`%, while region, island and season explain little or nothing.

```{r fig-time, fig.cap = "National real value per m² of new houses by quarter; the shaded area is the test period."}
include_graphics(fig("fig06_nz_quarterly_trend"))
```

## Which districts are dear or cheap?

```{r fig-rank, fig.cap = "Median relative cost by district, 1990–2019.", out.width = "85%"}
include_graphics(fig("fig08_district_ranking"))
```

Queenstown-Lakes, Wellington City, Thames-Coromandel, Lower Hutt, Porirua and Auckland were the dearest districts relative
to the rest of the country; Ōpōtiki, South Waikato, Selwyn, Horowhenua, Tararua and Ashburton the cheapest.

## Candidate drivers

```{r cor-table}
tab("t06_feature_correlations") |>
  rename(Feature = feature) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Correlation of each candidate predictor with the two responses (training rows)")
```

```{r fig-feat, fig.cap = "Relative cost against each candidate predictor, 1996–2019."}
include_graphics(fig("fig11_features_vs_relative_cost"))
```

Measures of building activity (alterations, number of new houses, dwellings per 1,000 residents, non-residential
work) and the share of multi-unit dwellings have the strongest, though modest, positive relationships with relative
cost. No single predictor has a correlation above 0.4.

```{r fig-conf, fig.cap = "House size and cost: raw (A) and compared within the same quarter (B)."}
include_graphics(fig("fig10_house_size_confounding"))
```

House size illustrates confounding. Across all years, larger houses appear dearer per m², but only because houses
and real costs both grew over time. Within the same quarter the relationship almost vanishes.

```{r fig-heat, fig.cap = "Correlations between candidate predictors."}
include_graphics(fig("fig12_feature_correlation_heatmap"))
```

The activity measures are strongly correlated with each other (variance inflation factors up to about 6), so linear
regression coefficients for them must be interpreted with care. Lasso and random-forest importance are better
guides to which matter.

## Train versus test

```{r fig-shift, fig.cap = "Distribution of each response in the training and test periods."}
include_graphics(fig("fig13_train_test_shift"))
```

```{r fig-persist, fig.cap = "Mean relative cost by district, training vs test period."}
include_graphics(fig("fig14_district_persistence"))
```

Real costs in 2020–2026 were about 17% higher than in the training years, a level that tree-based models cannot
predict because they only average training values. Relative costs barely shifted, and districts largely kept their
ranking (correlation 0.73).

## Decisions for modelling

* Main response: relative cost; secondary: log real $/m² with a time trend.
* Training window 1996–2019, so that all predictors are available without imputation.
* Island and season dropped; lagged costs excluded from the main (explanatory) models.

# RQ1: Models and results

```{r rq1-model-data}
cv   <- tab("t08_cv_results")
tst  <- tab("t09_test_results")
imp  <- tab("t10_variable_importance")
real <- tab("t11_real_response_results")
cvv <- function(m, s, col = "cv_rmse")   cv[[col]][cv$model == m & cv$set == s]
tv  <- function(m, s, col = "test_rmse") tst[[col]][tst$model == m & tst$set == s]
r3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
pc <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x, 1), "%")
```

## Approach

The main response is relative cost: the log of a district's real $/m² minus the log of the real $/m² of all other
districts in the same quarter. Models were trained on 1996–2019 (`r f0(sum(model$split == "train" & model$year >= 1996) - 2)`
district-quarters, after dropping Chatham Islands and Kawerau, which have only 1–2 usable rows). They were tested
once on 2020Q1–2026Q2.

We fitted eleven models in order of increasing flexibility:

* two baselines (the overall mean, and each district's own training mean);
* linear regression;
* polynomial regression;
* ridge, elastic net and lasso;
* a generalised additive model (GAM);
* a regression tree;
* a random forest;
* gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost);
* a support vector machine with a radial kernel.

Each model was fitted with two feature sets:

* **drivers**: nine measured features plus region and a city flag;
* **drivers + district**: the same nine features plus the district itself.

The drivers are:

* alteration spending;
* new houses;
* new dwellings per 1,000 residents;
* growth in house numbers;
* non-residential building;
* the shares of multi-unit, apartment and retirement dwellings;
* relative house size.

Every model's hyperparameters were tuned by **forward-chaining cross-validation** on the training years. There were
four folds, each training on all years before a two-year validation block (2012–13, 2014–15, 2016–17, 2018–19), so
no model ever saw the future. Models were compared on mean CV RMSE (log scale, ≈ proportional error). Among models
within one standard error of the best, the simplest was chosen.

```{r fig-folds, fig.cap = "Forward-chaining cross-validation folds within the training years."}
include_graphics(fig("fig15_cv_folds"))
```

## Cross-validation results

```{r cv-res-table}
cv |> mutate(set = recode(set, none = "-", drivers = "Drivers", district = "Drivers + district")) |>
  select(Set = set, Model = model, `Best settings` = best_settings, `CV RMSE` = cv_rmse, SE = cv_rmse_se,
         `CV R²` = cv_r2) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Cross-validated error of each model at its tuned settings (1996–2019).")
```

```{r fig-cv, fig.cap = "Cross-validated RMSE (±1 SE) of every model. Dashed line: district-mean baseline."}
include_graphics(fig("fig19_cv_comparison"))
```

**Drivers only:**

* The flexible models (random forest, XGBoost, SVM) do best, with CV R² ≈
  `r round(cvv("SVM (radial)", "drivers", "cv_r2"), 2)` versus ≈ `r round(cvv("Lasso", "drivers", "cv_r2"), 2)` for the
  linear family. So the drivers act non-linearly and interact.
* Even so, none clearly beats simply predicting each district's own average (CV RMSE
  `r r3(cvv("District mean", "none"))`).

**Drivers + district:**

* Penalised linear models are best (lasso CV RMSE `r r3(cvv("Lasso", "district"))`, R²
  `r round(cvv("Lasso", "district", "cv_r2"), 2)`), and they improve on the district mean.
* Once each district has its own level, the remaining effects of the drivers are close to additive and linear.

The one-standard-error rule selected a random forest (drivers set) and ridge regression (district set).

```{r fig-tree, fig.cap = "Regression tree on the drivers set (pruned for display). Red = dearer than the rest of NZ."}
include_graphics(fig("fig17_regression_tree"))
```

## Test-set performance (2020–2026)

```{r test-res-table}
tst |> mutate(set = recode(set, none = "-", drivers = "Drivers", district = "Drivers + district")) |>
  select(Set = set, Model = model, `Test RMSE` = test_rmse, `Test MAE` = test_mae, `Test R²` = test_r2,
         `MAPE ($/m²)` = test_mape) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Test-period performance, 2020Q1–2026Q2. MAPE is on real $/m².")
```

```{r fig-cvtest, fig.cap = "CV and test RMSE for each model. Dashed line: district-mean baseline on the test years."}
include_graphics(fig("fig20_cv_vs_test"))
```

All models, including the overall mean (`r r3(tv("Overall mean", "none"))` vs `r r3(cvv("Overall mean", "none"))` in CV),
have larger errors in 2020–26. Relative costs were more dispersed during the COVID period and the 2021–22 boom.

* The district set again beats the drivers set: best test R² ≈
  `r round(max(tst$test_r2[tst$set == "district"]), 2)` vs `r round(max(tst$test_r2[tst$set == "drivers"]), 2)`.
* The district-mean baseline remains hard to beat (MAPE `r pc(tv("District mean", "none", "test_mape"))`).
* The chosen ridge model predicts real $/m² with a mean absolute error of
  `r pc(tv("Ridge", "district", "test_mape"))`.

```{r fig-pva, fig.cap = "Predicted vs actual relative cost on the test years for the two chosen models."}
include_graphics(fig("fig21_test_pred_vs_actual"))
```

## What drives relative cost?

```{r fig-imp, fig.cap = "Variable importance from three models (drivers set). Colour shows the direction of the lasso coefficient."}
include_graphics(fig("fig22_variable_importance"))
```

Lasso coefficients, random-forest permutation importance and XGBoost gain agree on the main drivers:

* **Residential alteration spending** (positive) is the top driver: wealthier, busier markets build dearer houses.
* **Region:** broad location still matters.
* **New dwellings per 1,000 residents** (positive): fast-growing districts are dearer.
* **The number of new houses** (negative, holding the others fixed): high-volume, greenfield districts such as
  Selwyn are cheaper per m².
* **Relative house size** (negative): fixed costs are spread over more floor area.

The dwelling-mix shares contribute little. These are associations, not causal effects.

## Modelling real $/m² directly

```{r fig-real, fig.cap = "National geometric-mean real $/m² (black) and test-period predictions of models fitted to log real $/m² with a time trend."}
include_graphics(fig("fig23_real_cost_extrapolation"))
```

When the target is the real cost itself (with a time trend), each model family breaks down in its own way after
2019:

* the district mean under-predicts by about `r pc(-real$mean_bias[real$model == "District mean"])`;
* trees and forests flatten at the last level they saw;
* linear models extend the 1996–2019 trend and overshoot.

Modelling relative cost avoids having to forecast the national price level, which is why it is our main response.

# RQ1: Interpretation and answer

```{r rq1-interp-data}
eff <- tab("t12_effect_sizes")
wb  <- tab("t13_within_between")
bd  <- tab("t14_test_error_by_district")
ef  <- function(f, m) sprintf("%+.1f%%", eff[[m]][eff$feature == f])
```

## How each driver changes the prediction

```{r fig-pdp, fig.cap = "Partial dependence of predicted relative cost on six drivers, for the chosen random forest (drivers set), ridge on the same features, and the chosen ridge model with district. x-axis: percentile of the feature."}
include_graphics(fig("fig24_partial_dependence"))
```

A partial dependence curve shows how a model's average prediction changes as one feature moves while the others
keep their observed values. From the 10th to the 90th percentile of each feature:

* **Residential alteration spending** raises predicted relative cost by `r ef("log_resid_alt_real", "Random forest, drivers")`
  (random forest) to `r ef("log_resid_alt_real", "Ridge, drivers")` (ridge). All models agree and the curve is close to
  straight.
* **New dwellings per 1,000 residents** adds `r ef("dwell_per_1000", "Random forest, drivers")` in the forest, with a
  further jump of about 4% in the fastest-growing tenth of district-quarters.
* **House size, non-residential work and growth in house numbers** each move the prediction by 2% or less.

```{r fig-interaction, fig.cap = "Two-way partial dependence (random forest): alteration spending and growth together."}
include_graphics(fig("fig25_interaction_alterations_growth"))
```

The two leading drivers interact. Growth adds little where alteration spending is low, but up to about +14% where
spending is high. This is something additive models cannot represent, and it helps explain why the forest beat the
linear models on the drivers set.

## Between districts versus within a district

```{r within-between-table}
wb |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Feature", "Drivers set (between + within)", "District set (within only)", "Sign flips"),
            caption = "Ridge regression, standardised coefficients (log points per 1 SD).")
```

Adding the district to a model changes what the other coefficients mean. Without it, they mix comparisons between
districts with changes within a district over time. With it, only the within-district comparison remains.

* **Number of new houses** flips sign. For the same alteration spending and growth, districts that build many
  houses are cheaper per m² (volume builders, large subdivisions such as Selwyn), but a district is dearer in its
  own busier quarters (more demand for the same builders).
* **Dwellings per 1,000 residents** almost vanishes within districts. Fast-growing places are dearer, but a place is
  not much dearer in its own fast-growth years.
* **Alteration spending** keeps its sign and size, so it holds both between and within districts.

## Location premium left after the drivers

```{r fig-premium, fig.cap = "District premium before (raw average) and after accounting for the measured drivers (ridge, district set, 1996–2019)."}
include_graphics(fig("fig26_district_premium"))
```

The drivers explain only about a fifth of the variance between district averages. Queenstown-Lakes remains the
dearest district after its drivers (about +15% above the average district). Wellington City and Thames-Coromandel
lose about half their premium. Auckland and Christchurch move from dearer than average to cheaper than their drivers
predict, because they have the largest total alteration and non-residential spending in the country. This shows
that our activity features, which are total dollars, partly measure district size.

## Where the test predictions go wrong

```{r fig-error-year, fig.cap = "Test RMSE by year for the chosen models and the district-mean baseline, with the spread of actual relative costs (dashed)."}
include_graphics(fig("fig27_test_error_by_year"))
```

```{r fig-error-size, fig.cap = "Test RMSE by number of new houses in the district-quarter."}
include_graphics(fig("fig28_test_error_by_size"))
```

* Errors were smallest in 2020–2022 and largest in 2024, when the spread between districts peaked. Ridge beat the
  district-mean baseline in 2020–2023 but not in 2024–2026, so the relationships learned before 2020 drifted.
* All models under-predict by about 2–4% on average. Smaller districts became dearer relative to the large
  centres after 2020.
* Errors are largest for district-quarters with few houses, where one unusual consent moves the $/m².
* The largest errors in larger districts were in coastal and lifestyle areas (Kaipara, Thames-Coromandel, Western Bay
  of Plenty, Queenstown-Lakes), which became dearer than predicted, and in Waimakariri, which became cheaper.

A finer tuning grid for the random forest chose the same settings with no change in CV error, so these errors are
not a tuning problem.

## Answer to RQ1

**What drives the real cost per m² of new houses across districts?** Location matters most. The measured drivers
explain a modest part of it:

| Driver | Direction | Size (10th to 90th percentile) |
|---|---|---|
| Residential alteration spending | dearer | about +8% to +11% |
| Region | varies | up to about ±10% |
| Dwellings per 1,000 residents | dearer | about +3% to +6%, more in the fastest-growing places |
| Number of new houses | cheaper between districts (for the same alteration spending), dearer within | about ±5% |
| Relative house size | slightly cheaper | about −1% to −2% |
| Dwelling mix | none detected | under 1% |

With drivers and region only, the best models explain about a third of the variation in relative cost, about as
much as the district name alone. With the district added, ridge regression predicts 2020–2026 within about 8%
(MAPE), marginally better than each district's historical average. Most of the difference between districts lies in
features we do not observe: land, terrain, local labour markets and the type of house built.

# Discussion and limitations

**RQ1.**

* Consented value is the builder's estimate at consent time, not the final build cost, and it excludes land.
* The activity features are total dollars, so they partly measure district size. Per-resident versions would be
  cleaner, but population estimates are not in this release.
* We do not observe land prices, house specification or builder type, the most likely sources of the unexplained
  location premium.
* The results are associations in observational data, not causal effects.
* Auckland is treated as one district, and districts with fewer than five new houses in a quarter are left out, so
  the smallest districts are under-represented.
* Relationships drifted after 2023, so a model used for current decisions would need regular retraining.

*RQ2 and RQ3 points to be added.*
